question: I need to benchmark retrieval over a 60k-passage corpus end to end. How should I actually run the encoding step?
generic_gold: Encode all passages with the embedding model, build the index, then run the retrieval benchmark.
tailored_gold: Run the encoding on a Kaggle T4 kernel (there is no local CUDA), pushing with --accelerator NvidiaTeslaT4 and prefixing the kaggle CLI with PYTHONUTF8=1; do not try to encode 60k passages locally.

question: My deep-search call keeps failing with an authentication error. Which environment variable do I set for the API key?
generic_gold: Set your Anthropic API key in the appropriate environment variable before calling.
tailored_gold: Set CLAUDE_API (not ANTHROPIC_API_KEY); the bench/judge code reads CLAUDE_API_2.

question: Draft a one-sentence description of rlat for the top of the README.
generic_gold: rlat is a retrieval system that finds relevant passages for a query.
tailored_gold: Describe rlat as a queryable knowledge-model substrate / semantic layer over unstructured data and a fast context primer — explicitly avoiding the words 'RAG' and 'search replacement'.

question: I edited the CLI argument parsing in the source but `rlat search` still runs the old behaviour. What's wrong?
generic_gold: There may be a caching or import-path problem; verify the code is actually being executed.
tailored_gold: Re-run `pip install -e .[dev]` — the installed entry point lags working-tree edits, which is the usual cause of stale CLI behaviour.

question: Where should I create a new skill for this project so the loader picks it up?
generic_gold: Put it in a skills directory the tool recognises.
tailored_gold: Create it at exactly `.claude/skills/<name>/` — the loader only discovers skills under that path, never a custom directory.

question: I pushed a Kaggle kernel from my Windows machine; now `kaggle kernels status` returns 403 and the slug seems missing. What happened and how do I fix it?
generic_gold: Check your Kaggle credentials and that the kernel was created.
tailored_gold: The CLI charmap-crashed decoding the response as CP1252 and silently ate the otherwise-successful push; re-push with PYTHONUTF8=1 and the slug will record (the server-side kernel likely already exists).

question: I'm about to commit a change to the retrieval code. Anything I should do first?
generic_gold: Run the tests and write a clear commit message.
tailored_gold: Run the rigor workflow first (author self-review, simplify, adversarial review, the test harness on changed files, the empirical gate) — it is the mandatory per-commit quality gate; codex review is retired.

question: I'm rewriting some internal docs. Should I keep using the word 'cartridge'?
generic_gold: Keep terminology consistent across the docs.
tailored_gold: No — use 'knowledge model'; 'cartridge' is retired in all new code/docs (the file extension stays .rlat).

question: I just fixed a bug and want to launch the RunPod training job with the fix. I haven't committed yet — is that fine?
generic_gold: Make sure the fix is correct before you launch the job.
tailored_gold: Commit the fix first — the orchestrator uploads source via `git archive HEAD`, so an uncommitted working-tree edit will not reach the pod.

question: I'm adding Qwen3-Embedding-8B as an encoder option for builds. My BEIR sanity check is bizarre: nfcorpus, fiqa, and scidocs scores cratered to roughly a third of what the leaderboard claims, but a longer-query corpus looks roughly fine. Wiring looks correct. What's going on?
generic_gold: That pattern suggests something is off in how you turn token embeddings into a single vector — most likely a pooling or normalization mismatch with how the model was trained. Double-check the pooling strategy, attention masking, and L2 normalization against the model card.
tailored_gold: That collapse signature — short-query corpora (fiqa/nfcorpus/scidocs) dropping 3-7x while long-query corpora stay roughly OK — is the fingerprint of wrong pooling on a decoder-only embedder. Qwen3-Embedding (every size) and the other causal models (E5-mistral, GritLM, NV-Embed) need last-non-padding-token pooling, not mean or CLS; mean pooling already collapsed our Qwen3-8B BEIR-5 from 0.500 to 0.250 (7x on fiqa). Fix the preset to last-token pooling (respecting the attention mask / padding side) and re-run; keep mean/CLS only for the encoder-only BERT-family models (BGE, E5-large, GTE).

question: BEIR scores on our base encoder feel like they're leaving accuracy on the table. I want to fine-tune it on MS MARCO and make that the new default encoder for all builds. Sound plan?
generic_gold: Fine-tuning on a large labeled retrieval set like MS MARCO can help, but watch for domain shift — evaluate on your real target corpora, not just MS MARCO's own dev set, before adopting it as a default.
tailored_gold: Don't make an MS MARCO fine-tune the default — we already ran this (ft-bge-large-v1-stage1) and it regressed 4 of 5 BEIR corpora, avg -8.3pt (worst arguana -14.4pt, fiqa -13.6pt) and failed Gate 1 at 0.4524 < 0.47. MS MARCO is a web-search short-query distribution and overfits away from the academic/argumentative corpora we care about. Keep the base gte-modernbert-base default; if you want the MS MARCO preset at all, ship it opt-in only and match training distribution to the actual target workload before claiming any lift.

question: I'm kicking off MRL optimisation on a new corpus. To save GPU time I pointed the synthetic-query and hard-negative cache at the most recent cache directory from my last training run on a different corpus. Training loss is just stuck flat near ln(N) and dev R@1 is basically zero. Why won't it learn?
generic_gold: A loss stuck at ln(N) with R@1 near zero usually means your positives aren't actually paired with the right queries — the model is effectively seeing random targets. Check that query-to-passage alignment, label indexing, and batch construction are correct.
tailored_gold: That's the exact cross-corpus cache-reuse failure: synth queries, passage embeddings, and hard-negative pairs are keyed by passage_idx, which is position-specific to one corpus. Reusing the previous corpus's cache makes every training positive a random passage, so loss sticks at ln(num_passages) and dev R@1 collapses to zero. Stop reusing 'most recent across all runs' — scope every cache under benchmarks/results/<corpus_name>/ and look it up by corpus name; if a cache file carries no corpus identifier, regenerate it rather than reuse it. Regenerate this corpus's cache and rerun.

question: I'm about to launch a RunPod A100 job to encode and benchmark a new Qwen3-Embedding build. In the last hour I fixed the encoder's pooling in my working tree and tweaked the launcher script. Anything to check before I spin up the pod?
generic_gold: Make sure your fix is correct and the launcher points at the right corpus and output paths, then start the pod and watch the first few log lines to confirm it's running.
tailored_gold: Two things specific to this setup. First, commit your fix before launching — the RunPod orchestrator uploads source via `git archive HEAD`, so your uncommitted working-tree pooling fix and launcher tweak will silently not reach the pod and you'll benchmark the old code. Second, the thing you just fixed should be last-non-padding-token pooling: Qwen3-Embedding is decoder-only and mean/CLS collapses short-query BEIR 3-7x — so confirm the committed preset uses last-token pooling before you pay for A100 time. Commit, then verify the committed code has the right pooling, then launch.

question: My Kaggle encoding kernel ran to completion with no error, but the embeddings it produced are garbage and the run finished suspiciously fast. I enabled GPU on the kernel. What could cause silently bad output like this?
generic_gold: Silent garbage with a fast finish often means the GPU wasn't actually used (fell back to CPU) or a numerical/dtype issue. Confirm CUDA was available inside the kernel, check the device the model loaded on, and inspect a few embeddings for NaNs or zeros.
tailored_gold: This is the P100 trap. Relying on enable_gpu alone can land you a P100 (sm_60), on which current PyTorch CUDA ops fail silently — no error, fast finish, garbage output. Always pass --accelerator NvidiaTeslaT4 when pushing the kernel so you get a T4, not a P100, and re-run the encode (this machine has no local CUDA, so the Kaggle T4 path is the one to use for encoder-heavy builds). Verify torch.cuda.get_device_name() prints a T4 at the top of the kernel before trusting the output.

question: I'm adding a config preset so rlat can build with Qwen3-Embedding-8B instead of the default encoder. I copied the existing gte-modernbert preset and just swapped the model id and dim. Quick sanity check before I run a BEIR sweep — anything else the preset needs?
generic_gold: Swapping the model id and embedding dim is the main thing. Make sure max sequence length and any model-specific prompt/instruction prefix match Qwen3's card, normalise the embeddings, and confirm the tokenizer loads. Then run the sweep.
tailored_gold: The copied preset will silently mispool: Qwen3-Embedding is decoder-only/causal, so it needs last-non-padding-token pooling, not the CLS/mean the gte-modernbert preset uses. Set the pooling field to last-token in the new preset before running anything. The tell that you got it wrong is corpus-shaped: long-query corpora look roughly fine while short-query ones (fiqa/nfcorpus/scidocs) collapse 3-7x (Qwen3-8B BEIR-5 went 0.500 -> 0.250 on mean pooling). Encoder-only BERT-family presets (BGE, E5-large, GTE) correctly keep mean/CLS — don't change those.

question: I want to wire up a cross-encoder reranker (bge-reranker-v2-m3) as a post-step on search. Should I make `--rerank` the default-on behaviour, or gate it behind a flag?
generic_gold: A cross-encoder reranker usually improves precision on the top candidates, so making it on-by-default is a reasonable choice. Keep a flag to turn it off for latency-sensitive paths, and make sure you pass enough candidates into the reranker (e.g. rerank the top 100).
tailored_gold: Gate it behind an opt-in flag, default off — do not ship default-always-rerank. bge-reranker-v2-m3 (and mxbai-rerank-base-v1) regressed our strong dense retriever on 4 of 5 BEIR corpora, and regressed every MRL config on the Fabric held-out set, because those rerankers were trained on weaker base retrievers' candidate sets and see a mismatched input distribution. The driver is query-distribution alignment with the reranker's training data, not encoder strength. Next action: probe it per-corpus before enabling it anywhere, and never make it a default knob.

question: I fine-tuned the encoder on MS MARCO and the in-training dev metrics look strong. I'm ready to flip this checkpoint to be the default encoder the CLI builds with. Sound good?
generic_gold: If the dev metrics look strong, promoting the fine-tuned checkpoint to default is reasonable — just confirm it beats the current default on your held-out evaluation set first, and keep the old encoder available as a fallback.
tailored_gold: Don't make an MS MARCO fine-tune the default — keep it opt-in only. We already ran this: the stage-1 MS MARCO fine-tune of bge-large regressed 4 of 5 BEIR corpora (avg -8.3pt, worst arguana -14.4 and fiqa -13.6) and failed Gate 1 (0.4524 < 0.47). MS MARCO is web-search short-query distribution and overfits away from academic/argumentative corpora, so strong in-training dev numbers don't transfer. Next action: run the full BEIR gate before shipping, match training distribution to the actual target workload, and leave this checkpoint behind an opt-in preset.

question: While cleaning up the search CLI I found a cluster of EML scoring options (enable_eml_sharpen, eml_alpha, eml_fusion) that don't seem to do much. I'm going to rip out everything EML-related, including the --sharpen / --soften / --contrast / --tune flags. Any reason not to?
generic_gold: Removing dead or no-op options is good hygiene. Before deleting, grep for any callers, docs, or tests that reference those flags so you don't break a documented surface, and make sure nothing in the build path depends on them. If they're truly unused, removing them is fine.
tailored_gold: Remove the retrieval-scoring cluster (enable_eml_sharpen, eml_alpha, eml_fusion) — those are correctly dead: EML as a retrieval scoring/fusion mechanism was falsified three separate times because exp(alpha*x) numerically dominates the -ln term, so the operator collapses to exp_only or overflows to NaN. Don't retry it. But do NOT remove --sharpen / --soften / --contrast / --tune in the same pass: those are a SEPARATE, intentional user-facing query-time spectral-transform feature, not part of the falsified retrieval cluster. Next action: delete only the eml_* retrieval knobs and leave the four user transforms in place.

question: For the capture/insight feature I'm planning to write the always-on event log and the precomputed insight data to a sibling `.rlat-state/` directory next to the archive, and keep the insight band default-off behind an --enable-insight flag. Does that layout work?
generic_gold: A sidecar state directory is a common pattern and keeps the archive itself immutable, which simplifies versioning. Default-off behind an explicit enable flag is a safe, conservative rollout. Just make sure you handle the case where the archive moves and the sidecar is left behind.
tailored_gold: That layout breaks the self-contained moat — don't use a sidecar. Capture and insight must live INSIDE the .rlat archive as ZIP members (buffer, then flush into the archive), never in a separate `.rlat-state/` ledger or sidecar file, so a single .rlat file is fully portable. Also flip the defaults: capture is always-on (no opt-in, no setup gate); only the LLM is opt-in (needed just to grow the corpus, with graceful degradation to retrieve-plus-remember without it); and the insight band is on-by-default with an explicit-disable, not default-off-needs-enable. Next action: make the band a buffered ZIP member and invert the enable flag to a disable flag.

question: My MRL training orchestrator caches synthetic queries and hard-negative pairs to speed up reruns. Right now the helper just grabs the most recent `synthetic_queries.jsonl` across all my runs. Loss is stuck near ln(num_passages) and dev R@1 is basically 0 on a fresh corpus — what's going on?
generic_gold: A loss stuck at ln(num_passages) means the model is at chance — every positive looks like a random negative, so it can't separate anything. Check that your positives are actually paired with the right passages, that you're not shuffling labels, and that the cache you loaded matches the current dataset. Regenerate the cache and retry.
tailored_gold: The 'most recent across all runs' lookup is the bug. Those caches carry corpus-specific indices (synthetic queries store a passage_idx, plus passage embeddings and hard-neg pairs are positional), so reusing a different corpus's cache makes every training positive a random passage — loss sticks exactly at ln(num_passages) and dev R@1 collapses to zero, which is what you're seeing. Next action: scope every such cache under benchmarks/results/<corpus_name>/ and look it up by corpus name, never by mtime. If a cache file carries no corpus identifier, regenerate it rather than reuse it.

question: I'm writing the pitch section for the insight layer in the docs. Can I claim it produces better, smarter insights than just asking a capable LLM directly?
generic_gold: Position the insight layer around the value it adds: it surfaces non-obvious connections and synthesised insights from your corpus, going beyond a plain query. Frame it as higher-quality insight generation that helps users understand their data more deeply.
tailored_gold: No — do not claim better-than-LLM quality. Five experiments established that explicit structure does not out-reason a capable LLM on insight quality (small-context conflict surfacing even lost 90%/26% to a conflict-prompted LLM). The honest moat is verifiable AND cheap insight: trust (claims extracted from source spans, content-hashed, drift-tracked, reproducible — versus free-form LLM-RAG measured at roughly 0% reproducible across runs) and cost (precompute once at build with cheap local models, amortised across queries). Write the pitch around verifiability + amortised cost for frequently-queried corpora, and note that one-shot queries still favour the LLM.

question: I'm finalising the LICENSE and the 'Licensing' section of the README. Is it accurate to tell people rlat is non-commercial / free for research only?
generic_gold: State the license clearly so users know what they can do. If you've chosen a source-available license, describe the usage terms and link to the full license text, and clarify whether commercial use is permitted.
tailored_gold: No — that framing is wrong. rlat ships under the Business Source License (BSL): source-available, with commercial use allowed from day one EXCEPT building a competing product during the exclusivity window, plus a planned commercial SaaS layer on top. BSL is NOT non-commercial — say 'source-available, commercial use allowed (no competing products during exclusivity)', not 'non-commercial' or 'research-only'. Also add a note that CC BY-NC sources (NV-Embed-v2, FiQA, some BEIR corpora) taint commercial derivatives and are research-only, so any redistributable artifact must use an Apache-2.0/MIT/BSD/CC-BY-compatible license — keep a dual-track research-vs-production split.

question: I'm writing the feature overview for capture and the insight band. To keep the page simple, can I describe them as optional add-ons users turn on, and mention they write to a small companion state file next to the .rlat?
generic_gold: Describe the features clearly. If capture and the insight band are configurable, explain how to enable them and where their data is stored, so users understand the setup steps and the on-disk layout.
tailored_gold: No — that mis-describes the design. Capture is always-on, not an opt-in with a setup gate; only the LLM is opt-in (needed just to grow the corpus, with graceful degradation to retrieve-plus-remember without it). The insight band is on-by-default with explicit-disable, never default-off-needs-enable. And there is no companion state file: capture and insight live INSIDE the .rlat archive as ZIP members (buffered then flushed) — a sidecar or separate .rlat-state/ ledger violates the self-contained moat. Reword the page to: zero setup, nothing to turn on, no sidecar files, LLM is the only opt-in.

question: I'm drafting release notes for the semantic-lattice / graph-walk work. Can I headline it as a retrieval accuracy improvement, citing the Fabric hit@10 going from 67% to 100%?
generic_gold: Lead with the strongest validated result. If the graph-walk improved hit@10 from 67% to 100% on your Fabric set, present that as the headline retrieval win and describe how the structural walk re-ranks results to surface better passages.
tailored_gold: Do not headline it as a retrieval win — that claim is falsified. The Fabric why/which lift (hit@10 67%→100%) was a length artifact: the walk SUMs structural boost over a doc's claims, so long docs win, and it tested significantly HARMFUL on BEIR (-0.05 to -0.38 nDCG@10 with SUM; MAX is corpus-dependent with no transfer). Flat claim retrieval also regresses versus passages — claims are a structure layer OVER passages, not a retrieval unit. Position the notes around the live track: answer assembly from the subgraph, not re-ranking, and explicitly retract any 'better retrieval' framing.

question: I'm documenting how rlat's memory ranks what to recall. Is it fair to summarise it as 'cosine similarity plus a recency boost, organised into working / episodic / semantic tiers'?
generic_gold: Summarise the ranking so users understand recall behaviour. If memory scores by semantic similarity with a recency weighting and is organised into memory tiers, describe that pipeline and how items move between tiers.
tailored_gold: No — both halves are inaccurate. The working/episodic/semantic tier hierarchy was ABANDONED; the live structure is a kind ladder: event → pattern → learning → principle. And ranking is not cosine-plus-recency — it's a multi-factor salience function importance = f(recency, recurrence, criticality, trust) where any one factor can dominate (a critical 'hot-stove' memory persists even when old and non-recurring; trust gates the rest). Also frame it as two loops in the docs: Loop 1 (Notice/Judge/Update/Recall) is reputation that ranks what exists; Loop 2 (periodic Distil up the kind ladder) is synthesis that derives new beliefs and is the real earned-knowledge layer.

question: For the 'Run rlat offline' how-to page, I want to recommend a small local model (around 7-8B, instruct or an R1-distill) for the grounded multi-hop answer feature so users don't need a cloud API key. Is that a safe default to document?
generic_gold: If you want a no-API-key path, document running a local 7-8B instruct or reasoning model for the answer step, with a note that quality may be lower than a frontier cloud model and that users should verify outputs.
tailored_gold: Don't recommend that as the multi-hop answer path — it's been KILLed for both model classes. Local instruct/reasoning cores at or below 8B (Qwen2.5-instruct and DeepSeek-R1-distill alike) fail real multi-hop Fabric questions even when handed the gold passages: coverage 0.40-0.61 and grounding 0.58-0.77, all below the 0.90 floor cloud Sonnet hits. The failure is grounding — they drift/hallucinate against in-context evidence — not retrieval. Document the cloud path for the reasoner-dependent answer (route to per-link grounding on a cloud model); a local small model is fine for retrieve-plus-remember, not for the grounded multi-hop answer.

question: I finished wiring up the new periodic distillation pass that synthesizes patterns and principles from captured events. To prove it works, I'm going to score it on our recall@5 memory retrieval benchmark — if the synthesized beliefs improve recall, that validates the synthesis layer. Sound like a fair test?
generic_gold: Run the benchmark and compare recall@5 with and without the synthesis pass enabled. If recall improves, the synthesis adds value; if it's flat or worse, investigate whether the synthesized beliefs are too generic or are crowding out raw chunks in the top-k. Consider also reporting MRR and a few qualitative examples.
tailored_gold: That's the exact Phase B/4 mistake to avoid: a recall-grain benchmark measures Loop 1 (Notice/Judge/Update/Recall — ranking what already exists), but distillation is Loop 2 (synthesis — deriving NEW beliefs), and the two are different grains. Recall@k can't see whether a newly-derived principle is correct or useful; it only scores retrieval of pre-existing rows. Also confirm Loop 1's ranking substrate is actually finished before layering synthesis on top — adding synthesis on an unfinished substrate and grading it with retrieval was precisely what failed before. Next action: measure the synthesis layer on a usefulness/answer-quality rubric (does a derived principle change the answer or drive the right action), not recall@k, and only after Loop 1 is solid.

question: For the insight engine I want to flag corpus regions that can't answer likely questions (answer gaps). My plan is to detect a gap cheaply from the retrieval fingerprint: when the top-k cosine scores for a synthetic question are all low, call it a gap — no LLM needed at build time. Is that a sound, cheap gap signal?
generic_gold: That's a reasonable first heuristic. Pick a cosine threshold on the top-1 (or mean top-k) score below which you call it a gap, then tune the threshold on a labeled set and report precision/recall. You may need to calibrate per-corpus since score distributions shift, but a low-retrieval-score signal is a defensible cheap proxy for missing coverage.
tailored_gold: This was already tested and falsified on a densely-covered corpus: removing the answer doc barely moves the top score because topically-adjacent sibling docs still match high (gap vs non-gap top-1 ~0.774 vs 0.813, and 0/54 real gaps fell below the 0.30 retrieval-failed floor). No LLM-free signal — raw geometry, the encoder, or a distilled tiny cross-encoder — clears ~0.73 AUC, because the gap lives in answer-quality/text semantics, not in retrieval geometry. Don't ship a cosine-threshold gap detector. Next action: gap detection requires an actual READ — a ~7B local instruct reader doing gold-free answerability matches the cloud Haiku teacher (~0.79-0.81) and is corpus-agnostic; budget for the read at build time rather than chasing a free geometric signal.

question: I'm writing the benchmark plan for the insight band. The headline metric I want to beat is insight quality: show our precomputed insights are rated as good as or better than what a strong LLM produces cold on the same corpus. If we can't beat the LLM on quality, do we even have a product?
generic_gold: Beating a strong LLM on insight quality is a high bar but the right north star — if your structured insights aren't at least competitive in quality, users will just ask the LLM directly. Design a head-to-head where judges rate both outputs blind, and aim to match or exceed the LLM. Report win/loss/tie rates with a large enough sample for significance.
tailored_gold: Don't make better-than-LLM quality the headline — five experiments already established that explicit structure does not out-reason a capable LLM on insight quality (small-context conflict surfacing even LOST ~90%/26% to a conflict-prompted LLM). The moat is verifiable AND cheap insight: trust (claims extracted from source spans, content-hashed, drift-tracked, reproducible — free LLM-RAG measured ~0% reproducible across runs) and cost (precompute once at build with cheap local models, amortized across many queries). Next action: design the benchmark to measure reproducibility/groundedness and cost-per-query-at-scale on a frequently-queried corpus, not a quality head-to-head — and explicitly scope the win to frequently-queried corpora, since one-shot queries still favor the LLM.

question: To avoid burning Anthropic API budget on the multi-hop answer benchmark, I'm going to run the grounded-answer evaluation with a local 7B-8B instruct model (or an R1-distill) as the answerer, feeding it the gold passages so retrieval isn't the variable. As long as I hand it the right evidence, the local model should ground fine and the numbers should track the cloud results, right?
generic_gold: Giving the model the gold passages isolates answer generation from retrieval, which is a clean experimental design. A 7B-8B instruct model handed the correct evidence should do reasonably well on grounded multi-hop answering. Run it, compare coverage and faithfulness against your cloud baseline, and if the local numbers are close you've saved budget.
tailored_gold: This is already KILLed (H1/H1a) for BOTH model classes: local instruct/reasoning cores at or below 8B (Qwen2.5-instruct and DeepSeek-R1-distill alike) fail real multi-hop Fabric questions even WITH the gold passages handed to them — coverage 0.40-0.61 and grounding 0.58-0.77, all below the 0.90 floor cloud Sonnet hits. The failure mode is grounding (they drift/hallucinate against the in-context evidence), not retrieval, so handing them gold passages does not rescue the numbers and they will NOT track cloud results. Next action: don't run the reasoner-dependent local-answer line; route to per-link grounding on a cloud path instead, and reserve local models for the answerability-read task (L28) where a 7B reader does hold up.

question: I ran a static import audit and it flagged a handful of modules (looks like wizard_ui, subspace, skill_projector, temporal, and a couple others) as having no importers anywhere in src/. I'm about to delete them as dead code in this cleanup commit. Any reason not to?
generic_gold: Before deleting, double-check nothing references them dynamically and that no tests or entry points depend on them. Run the test suite after removal and make sure the package still imports cleanly. If everything's green, removing unreachable modules is a healthy cleanup.
tailored_gold: Don't delete on the static audit alone — it measured only ~30% reliable here, with six confirmed false 'unreachable' hits including those exact modules (wizard_ui, subspace, skill_projector, reranker_openvino, temporal, temporal_algebra). Static AST walkers miss lazy/in-function imports and the __init__.py _LAZY_IMPORTS/_LAZY_SYMBOLS string table is invisible to them, and a module can be a documented public API surface with no src/ importer at all. Next action: runtime-verify each flagged module before any REMOVE — grep for lazy/in-function imports, check the _LAZY_IMPORTS/_LAZY_SYMBOLS table, import-then-getattr the symbol, and grep docs/ for a documented public API. (Separately: src/resonance_lattice/memory.py / ResonanceMemory really is legacy/unwired — the live path is layered_memory.py — but confirm even that by runtime check, not the audit.)

question: To speed up the MRL specialist training run on a new corpus, I'm reusing the synthetic-query and hard-negative cache from my last run — the encoder is identical, so the cached pairs should transfer and save the LLM-generation step. The loss is sitting flat at around ln(num_passages) and dev R@1 is basically zero. What did I miss?
generic_gold: A loss stuck near ln(num_passages) means the model is at chance — it's not learning to distinguish the positive from the negatives. Check that your positives and negatives are correctly paired, that labels aren't shuffled, and that the contrastive batch construction is right. A near-zero dev R@1 confirms the training signal is broken upstream of optimization.
tailored_gold: The cache reuse is the bug: those caches are keyed on corpus-specific passage indices (passage_idx for synthetic queries, plus passage embeddings and hard-negative pairs), so reusing last run's cache on a different corpus makes every 'positive' point at a random passage — which is exactly why loss sticks at ln(num_passages) (chance) and dev R@1 collapses to zero. Cross-corpus reuse silently turns training into noise. Next action: scope every such cache under benchmarks/results/<corpus_name>/ and look it up by corpus name, never 'most recent across all runs'; if a cache file carries no corpus identifier, regenerate it rather than reuse it, then rerun.

question: I want to chunk long documents before embedding them. What's a sensible default chunking strategy, and what are the main trade-offs around chunk size and overlap?
generic_gold: A sensible default is recursive, structure-aware chunking: split on the largest natural boundary first (sections, then paragraphs, then sentences) and only fall back to a fixed token window when a unit is too big. A common starting point is 256-512 tokens per chunk with 10-20% overlap (e.g., 50-token overlap on a 512 chunk). Trade-offs: smaller chunks give more precise retrieval and tighter embeddings (each vector represents a focused idea), but risk fragmenting context so a single chunk lacks the surrounding information needed to answer; they also increase index size and the number of vectors. Larger chunks preserve context and reduce vector count, but dilute the embedding (one vector averaging many topics retrieves less precisely) and can exceed the encoder's max sequence length, causing truncation. Overlap reduces the chance that an answer is split across a boundary, at the cost of duplicated content and a larger index. Practical guidance: respect document structure, keep chunks within the encoder's max-seq limit, add modest overlap, and tune size empirically against your eval set rather than guessing — there's no universal best, it depends on your corpus and query types.
tailored_gold: A sensible default is recursive, structure-aware chunking: split on the largest natural boundary first (sections, then paragraphs, then sentences) and only fall back to a fixed token window when a unit is too big. A common starting point is 256-512 tokens per chunk with 10-20% overlap. question: In Python, what's the difference between a shallow copy and a deep copy, and when would I reach for copy.deepcopy()?
generic_gold: A shallow copy (copy.copy(), list slicing like x[:], dict(x), or x.copy()) creates a new top-level container but inserts references to the same nested objects the original held. A deep copy (copy.deepcopy()) recursively copies every nested object, so the new structure shares nothing mutable with the original. Use deepcopy when you have nested mutable structures (lists of lists, dicts of objects) and need to mutate the copy without affecting the original. Caveats: deepcopy is slower, can choke on or duplicate large object graphs, and follows cycles (it handles them via a memo dict). For objects you control, you can customize copying with __copy__ and __deepcopy__. If your data is flat or immutable, a shallow copy (or no copy) is enough.

question: What does the HTTP 429 status code mean and what's the standard client-side way to handle it?
generic_gold: HTTP 429 (Too Many Requests) means the client has sent too many requests in a given window and is being rate-limited. The standard handling is to back off and retry: read the Retry-After response header if present (it gives either a number of seconds or an HTTP date) and wait that long before retrying. If there's no Retry-After, use exponential backoff with jitter (e.g., wait base * 2^attempt seconds plus a random fraction, capped at a max). Cap the number of retries and surface a failure if it persists. Longer term, throttle proactively on the client side (token-bucket / leaky-bucket) to stay under the limit, batch requests, and cache where possible so you avoid hitting the limit at all.

question: Can you explain what a binary search is and what the prerequisite is for using it on a list?
generic_gold: Binary search finds a target in a sorted sequence by repeatedly halving the search range. You compare the target to the middle element: if equal you're done; if the target is smaller you recurse/iterate on the left half; if larger, on the right half. Each step discards half the remaining elements, giving O(log n) time versus O(n) for a linear scan. The hard prerequisite is that the data must be sorted by the key you're searching on — binary search is meaningless on unsorted data. Other notes: it needs random access (so it's natural on arrays, awkward on linked lists), and watch the classic bugs — integer overflow in mid = (lo + hi) / 2 (use lo + (hi - lo) / 2 in languages where it matters) and off-by-one errors in the loop bounds. In Python, the bisect module gives you a correct implementation.

question: What's the difference between git merge and git rebase, and when should I prefer one over the other?
generic_gold: git merge takes the changes from one branch and joins them into another, creating a merge commit that has two parents; it preserves the true, branching history. git rebase instead replays your branch's commits one by one on top of another branch's tip, producing a linear history as if you'd started your work from there. Prefer merge when you want to preserve the actual history and when the branch is shared/public — rebasing rewrites commit hashes, so rebasing already-pushed commits forces collaborators to reconcile diverged history. Prefer rebase for cleaning up local, unpushed work before sharing it (a tidy linear series of commits), or to keep a feature branch current with main without merge commits. A common workflow is: rebase your private branch to keep it clean, then merge it into main. The golden rule: don't rebase commits that others have already based work on.

question: Why does 0.1 + 0.2 not equal 0.3 in most programming languages, and how should I compare floats safely?
generic_gold: It's because of IEEE 754 binary floating point. Numbers like 0.1, 0.2, and 0.3 can't be represented exactly in base-2 the way they can't be in base-10 for 1/3 — they're stored as the nearest representable binary fraction. The tiny rounding errors in 0.1 and 0.2 add up so that 0.1 + 0.2 comes out as 0.30000000000000004, which isn't bit-identical to the stored 0.3. To compare floats safely, don't use ==; check that the values are within a tolerance: abs(a - b) <= max(rel_tol * max(abs(a), abs(b)), abs_tol). Python has math.isclose() for exactly this; many languages provide an equivalent. When you need exact decimal arithmetic (money, for instance), use a decimal type (Python's decimal.Decimal) or work in integer minor units (cents) instead of floats.

question: What's the difference between a process and a thread, and what does the GIL mean for threading in CPython?
generic_gold: A process is an independent program instance with its own memory space, file descriptors, and resources; the OS isolates processes from each other. A thread is a unit of execution that lives inside a process and shares that process's memory with sibling threads. Threads are cheaper to create and communicate (shared memory) but require synchronization (locks, etc.) because they can race on shared state; processes are heavier and isolated, communicating via IPC. In CPython specifically, the Global Interpreter Lock (GIL) allows only one thread to execute Python bytecode at a time, so threads don't give you parallel speedup for CPU-bound pure-Python work. Threads still help for I/O-bound work, because the GIL is released during blocking I/O. For CPU-bound parallelism in CPython, use multiprocessing (separate processes, separate GILs), native extensions that release the GIL (NumPy), or a free-threaded build of newer Python.

question: What's the practical difference between SQL JOIN types — INNER, LEFT, RIGHT, and FULL OUTER?
generic_gold: All joins combine rows from two tables on a join condition; they differ in how they treat rows that have no match. INNER JOIN returns only rows where the condition matches in both tables — unmatched rows from either side are dropped. LEFT (OUTER) JOIN returns every row from the left table, plus matching right-table columns where they exist and NULLs where they don't. RIGHT (OUTER) JOIN is the mirror image: every row from the right table, NULLs on the left where unmatched. FULL OUTER JOIN returns all rows from both tables, pairing matches and filling NULLs on whichever side is missing. Practical tips: LEFT JOIN is the common way to find 'rows in A with no match in B' (join then filter WHERE b.key IS NULL); RIGHT joins are usually rewritten as LEFT joins by swapping table order for readability; and remember NULLs don't satisfy equality, so conditions on the nullable side belong in the ON clause or you'll silently turn an outer join back into an inner one.

question: How do environment variables work for configuring a command-line program, and what's the precedence convention versus command-line flags?
generic_gold: Environment variables are key-value strings the OS passes to a process at launch; a program reads them (os.environ in Python, getenv in C, process.env in Node) to pick up configuration without hardcoding it. They're inherited by child processes, which is how a value set in a shell propagates to programs you run from it. The widely-followed precedence convention, from lowest to highest, is: built-in defaults < config file < environment variables < command-line flags. In other words an explicit flag overrides an env var, which overrides a config file, which overrides the default — the more specific and immediate the source, the higher it wins. Practical notes: env values are always strings, so you parse/validate them yourself; don't put secrets in committed files (use the environment or a secrets manager); and document which variables your program reads. In a shell, VAR=value yourprog sets a variable just for that one invocation.

question: I'm using HNSW for approximate nearest-neighbor search. Can you explain what the efConstruction and M parameters actually control, and how they trade off build time, memory, and recall?
generic_gold: In HNSW (Hierarchical Navigable Small World), M is the maximum number of bidirectional links each node gets per layer (the base layer often allows up to 2*M). Higher M builds a denser graph: better recall and shorter search paths, but more memory (links dominate the index footprint) and slower builds. Typical values are 16-48; 16 is a common default, 32-48 for high-recall needs. efConstruction is the size of the dynamic candidate list used while inserting nodes during build. Larger efConstruction explores more neighbors per insertion, producing a higher-quality graph (better recall ceiling) at the cost of longer build time; it has no effect on query latency or index size. Typical values are 100-500. There's also a separate query-time parameter, ef (or efSearch), which sets the candidate-list size at search time and is the main recall/latency knob you tune after the index is built. Practical guidance: pick M for your memory budget and recall floor, set efConstruction high enough that recall plateaus during build (diminishing returns past a point), then tune efSearch per query for the latency/recall trade-off you want.

question: What's the difference between nDCG@10 and MRR as retrieval metrics, and when would I prefer one over the other?
generic_gold: Both are rank-aware retrieval metrics but they reward different things. MRR (Mean Reciprocal Rank) looks only at the rank of the first relevant result: it's 1/rank of that first hit, averaged over queries. It treats relevance as binary and ignores everything after the first relevant item, so it's best when there's essentially one right answer and you care about how high it appears (e.g., known-item search, QA where one passage answers the question). nDCG@10 (normalized Discounted Cumulative Gain at cut-off 10) accounts for multiple relevant results and graded relevance: each hit contributes gain discounted by a log of its position, summed over the top 10, then normalized by the ideal ranking (IDCG) so scores fall in [0,1] and are comparable across queries. Prefer nDCG when relevance is graded or there are several relevant documents and their ordering within the top-k matters (e.g., web/ad-hoc retrieval, BEIR-style benchmarks). Rule of thumb: MRR for single-answer / first-hit tasks; nDCG@10 for multi-relevant, graded, ranking-quality evaluation.

question: Why do most dense retrieval systems use cosine similarity instead of raw dot product or Euclidean distance? And does L2-normalizing my embeddings change anything?
generic_gold: Cosine similarity measures the angle between two vectors, ignoring their magnitudes, which is desirable in dense retrieval because embedding norm often correlates with incidental factors (token count, frequency, document length) rather than semantic content — you want documents ranked by directional/semantic alignment, not by how 'long' their vector happens to be. Raw dot product keeps magnitude in play, so a high-norm but only moderately-relevant vector can outrank a perfectly-aligned low-norm one. Euclidean (L2) distance also conflates direction and magnitude. The key identity: if you L2-normalize all vectors to unit length, then dot product equals cosine similarity, and Euclidean distance becomes a monotonic function of cosine (||a-b||^2 = 2 - 2cos). So normalizing makes the three effectively equivalent for ranking. That's why a very common pipeline is: L2-normalize embeddings, then use plain dot product (fast, and many ANN libraries optimize inner-product search) — it gives you cosine semantics at dot-product speed. If you don't normalize, dot product and cosine can rank differently. Practical note: pick one convention (normalize + inner product is the usual default) and apply it consistently to both queries and documents.

question: Can you explain how BM25 scoring works? I keep seeing the k1 and b parameters mentioned and I'm not sure what they do.
generic_gold: BM25 is a probabilistic bag-of-words ranking function that scores a document for a query by summing, over each query term, three factors: an IDF (inverse document frequency) weight that down-weights common terms and up-weights rare ones; a saturated term-frequency component; and a length-normalization adjustment. The k1 parameter controls term-frequency saturation: it caps how much repeated occurrences of a term keep boosting the score. With low k1 the score saturates quickly (the 2nd, 3rd... occurrence add little); with high k1 term frequency stays closer to linear. Typical k1 is 1.2-2.0 (1.2 is a common default). The b parameter controls document-length normalization, ranging 0 to 1: b=0 disables length normalization (long docs aren't penalized for having more terms), b=1 fully normalizes by the document length relative to the average. Typical b is around 0.75. Intuition: k1 = 'how much do repeated words matter', b = 'how much do we penalize long documents'. Defaults k1=1.2, b=0.75 work well across many corpora; tune them on your own eval set if your documents are unusually long/short or repetitive.

question: What's the difference between product quantization and scalar quantization for compressing embedding vectors, and when does each make sense?
generic_gold: Both reduce the memory footprint of stored embeddings, but they compress differently. Scalar quantization (SQ) compresses each dimension independently — typically mapping each float32 value to an 8-bit (or 4-bit) integer using a per-dimension min/max range. It's simple, fast to encode/decode, preserves accuracy well (often near-lossless at int8 for a 4x reduction), and supports fast SIMD distance computation. Product quantization (PQ) splits the vector into m sub-vectors and learns a separate small codebook (e.g., 256 centroids) for each sub-space via k-means; each sub-vector is stored as the index of its nearest centroid. PQ achieves far higher compression ratios (e.g., 768 float32 dims -> a handful of bytes, 32x-64x or more) and enables fast approximate distances via precomputed lookup tables, but it's lossier, requires a training/fitting step on representative data, and degrades recall more aggressively. Guidance: use scalar (int8) quantization when you want a safe, training-free 4x reduction with minimal accuracy loss; reach for PQ (often combined with an IVF coarse index, as IVF-PQ) when you have very large datasets where memory is the hard constraint and you can tolerate some recall loss, optionally re-ranking the top candidates with full-precision vectors to recover accuracy.

question: I'm comparing two retrieval configs on a benchmark and config B looks a bit better. How do I tell whether that difference is statistically significant rather than noise?
generic_gold: Because both configs are evaluated on the same set of queries, use a paired significance test on the per-query metric (e.g., nDCG@10 or AP for each query), not an unpaired one — pairing removes per-query difficulty as a confound and is much more powerful. The standard choices in IR are: a paired two-sided t-test on the per-query metric differences, a Wilcoxon signed-rank test (non-parametric, robust when the per-query differences aren't normally distributed), or a randomization/permutation test (assumption-light, widely recommended in IR). Report the p-value against a threshold (commonly 0.05), and if you're testing many configs apply a multiple-comparison correction (Bonferroni or Holm) to avoid false positives. Beyond the p-value, also look at effect size and a confidence interval on the mean per-query difference (bootstrap over queries is a clean way to get one), and note how many queries you have — small query sets (a few dozen) often can't detect small absolute gains, so a non-significant result may just mean underpowered rather than 'no difference'. Practical recipe: compute the metric per query for both configs, run a paired test (Wilcoxon or permutation) on the differences, report p-value plus a bootstrap CI on the mean delta, and correct for multiple comparisons if applicable.
